summary: A satirical opinion piece examining the recycling incentive programs launched by local governments as of September 1, 2023, which reward residents with cash, points, coupons and prizes. It uses anecdotes about residents gaming or chasing rewards to question whether paying people to recycle builds a lasting culture of recycling. It notes a slight uptick in recycling but worries about what happens when incentives end.
one_line: A satirical look at local recycling incentive programs, questioning whether rewards for recycling create lasting environmental responsibility or just pragmatic prize-chasing.
key_facts: As of September 1, 2023, local governments and councils launched incentive programs to increase recycling rates among residents.
Maya Cleary, Director of Environmental Initiatives, is described as the scheme's architect and said, "We're not bribing you to care for the planet, we're encouraging you!"
Rewards include cash, points, coupons and prizes; the programs run from September through November and are gamified with point tallies.
Joe Smith, an avid soda drinker, said he never used the blue bin before but might not now unless there is something in it for him; he held a ticket to the local zoo.
Jane Doe, a local influencer, said she was "just 200 points away from the blender!"
Frank "Bins" McGee, a long-time conservationist, complained that people now need a bribe via an app, recalling when people used both sides of the paper.
Preliminary reports since the system began suggest a slight uptick in recycling, which the article says is matched by skeptics' angst.
A main concern is what happens when the incentives run out and whether waste habits will backslide.
Tony "Two Bins" Genaro wants seven identical blenders and rifles through neighbors' rubbish for recyclables, spiking recycling metrics and prompting a neighborhood watch program.
Timmy, age 9, sorts recyclables daily hoping to earn a Disney World trip, but his family calculates he'd reach the goal around the turn of the next century.
The article says creativity has bloomed and trash panda populations are bewildered by cleaner dumpsters, but calls the programs possibly a Band-Aid on a bullet wound.
The author concludes the programs lure people into responsible citizenship through pragmatism and prizes rather than morality.
